title: Leg 55 — Geysers, Yellowstone Lake, and Tetons
subtitle: Madison Junction, Grand Prismatic, Old Faithful, West Thumb, Yellowstone Lake and the Tetons
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. Today we're leaving West Yellowstone and making a southbound tour through the heart of Yellowstone before continuing into Grand Teton National Park. We'll pass Madison Junction, Grand Prismatic Spring, Old Faithful, West Thumb and Yellowstone Lake, then follow the south entrance corridor toward Jackson Lake and the Tetons. This leg mixes the scenery with visitor culture, park history and a few of Yellowstone's stranger human stories. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: Leaving West Yellowstone
blocks.text: West Yellowstone is dropping behind us as we cross into the park. This little gateway town exists largely because millions of people want access to Yellowstone, and the contrast is immediate: hotels, restaurants and traffic give way to forest, rivers and a road network built around sightseeing.

blocks.title: One of America's busiest national parks
blocks.text: Yellowstone recorded about 4.76 million recreation visits in 2025, making it the third most visited national park that year. July alone was just under a million visits. From the airplane, that visitor pressure is mostly invisible, but down on the roads it can turn a wildlife sighting into an instant traffic jam.

blocks.title: Before the family road trip
blocks.text: Early visitors had a very different vacation. Many arrived by train and then spent days riding stagecoaches and Yellowstone wagons from hotel to hotel. Drivers with nicknames like Crying Jack and Society Red entertained tourists with frontier stories while the passengers bounced around the park.

blocks.title: Madison Junction
blocks.text: Madison Junction is just ahead where the Gibbon and Firehole rivers join to form the Madison. It is one of those places where Yellowstone's road system and river system meet in an easy-to-read landscape, and it marks our turn toward the geyser basins.

blocks.title: Into the geyser basin country
blocks.text: We're heading south into one of the most hydrothermally active corridors on Earth. Steam plumes can be easier to spot than individual pools from this altitude, especially on a cool day.

blocks.title: Grand Prismatic coming up
blocks.text: Grand Prismatic Spring is coming up off the left side. It should become a strong visual target before we're abeam because the spring is huge and its orange, yellow and green microbial mats contrast sharply with the surrounding basin.

blocks.title: Yellowstone's largest hot spring
blocks.text: Grand Prismatic is Yellowstone's largest hot spring, roughly two to three hundred feet across and more than 120 feet deep. The vivid colors are not decorative minerals painted around the edge; much of that color comes from heat-loving microorganisms living at different temperature zones.

blocks.title: The Midway Geyser Basin view
blocks.text: This is the best part of the pass for Grand Prismatic. Keep looking left for the broad turquoise center, the orange-brown runoff apron and the steam drifting over Midway Geyser Basin. Even if steam hides the center, the enormous colored footprint should help locate it.

blocks.title: Old Faithful is next
blocks.text: Old Faithful and the Upper Geyser Basin are only a few miles ahead, off the left side. If the geyser happens to erupt while we're passing, that's luck rather than timing; its current median interval is a little over 100 minutes.

blocks.title: The crowd waiting for one geyser
blocks.text: On the ground, Old Faithful turns waiting into a group activity. Hundreds or sometimes thousands of visitors can gather around the viewing area, all watching the same patch of ground for the eruption to begin. The geyser typically reaches around 130 feet, though individual eruptions can be much taller.

blocks.title: A hotel built to match the landscape
blocks.text: Beside the geyser is Old Faithful Inn, opened in 1904. Its enormous log lobby, local stone and deliberately rustic design helped define the architectural style people now associate with classic national park lodges. Early guests even dressed for dinner and danced to a string quartet six nights a week.

blocks.title: Old Faithful off the left
blocks.text: We're passing the Old Faithful area now. Look left for the dense complex of buildings, boardwalks and thermal clearings. If there is a tall white plume rising suddenly from the basin, you may have caught an eruption; otherwise the basin itself is still the landmark.

blocks.title: Leaving the Upper Geyser Basin
blocks.text: Old Faithful is moving behind-left as we climb toward Craig Pass. Yellowstone has far more hydrothermal features than its famous names suggest, so the steam pockets scattered through the valleys are part of a much larger system.

blocks.title: When cars changed Yellowstone
blocks.text: Automobiles were not officially allowed into Yellowstone until 1915. Park managers had resisted them, partly because early cars and horse-drawn traffic mixed badly. Once cars arrived, visitation surged and the park had to adapt its roads, services and visitor facilities to a new kind of tourism.

blocks.title: Craig Pass
blocks.text: Craig Pass is just ahead, carrying us across the high divide toward West Thumb. The pass is less a single spectacular landmark than a transition: geyser-basin country falls behind and Yellowstone Lake suddenly becomes the next enormous visual anchor.

blocks.title: Yellowstone Lake ahead
blocks.text: Yellowstone Lake should be opening ahead now, broad enough to feel almost out of scale with the surrounding plateau. West Thumb is the western bay, and our next pass brings thermal features right to the edge of that cold alpine water.

blocks.title: A caldera inside the larger caldera
blocks.text: West Thumb is itself a volcanic caldera formed roughly 174,000 years ago, nested inside the larger Yellowstone volcanic system. The basin later filled with lake water, so here hot springs, geysers and lake shoreline occupy the same piece of landscape.

blocks.title: The place tourists once cooked fish on the hook
blocks.text: West Thumb also produced one of Yellowstone's strangest tourist traditions. At Fishing Cone, visitors once caught trout from the cold lake and swung the fish directly into the hot spring to cook it on the hook. It became such a famous stunt that tourists posed in cook's hats and aprons. The practice is now prohibited.

blocks.title: West Thumb along the shoreline
blocks.text: This is the West Thumb viewing pass. Look along the lake edge for pale thermal ground, pools and steam beside the much darker water. The contrast between near-boiling hydrothermal features and a lake that averages only about 41 degrees is one of the oddest juxtapositions in Yellowstone.

blocks.title: Across Yellowstone Lake
blocks.text: We're following the southern part of Yellowstone Lake now. At about 7,733 feet elevation, it is the largest high-elevation lake above 7,000 feet in North America, roughly 20 miles long and 14 miles wide.

blocks.title: Beautiful water that stays dangerously cold
blocks.text: The lake looks inviting from the air, but it stays cold enough that swimming is a bad idea. The National Park Service puts the average water temperature around 41 degrees, with estimated survival time in the water often only 20 to 30 minutes.

blocks.title: A lake used for thousands of years
blocks.text: Archaeological sites around Yellowstone Lake show that Native peoples used this area for thousands of years for travel, hunting, fishing and seasonal life. The modern park road is only the latest transportation layer around a lake that has long been important to people.

blocks.title: Yellowstone Lake South Arm
blocks.text: The broad South Arm is close now. Take in the scale rather than looking for a single object: open water, forested shoreline and high plateau country all spread out together before the route turns toward the south entrance.

blocks.title: South toward the park entrance
blocks.text: We're leaving the open lake and moving into a narrower forested corridor toward Yellowstone's south entrance. The landscape becomes more intimate again, with rivers and roads squeezed between wooded slopes.

blocks.title: The road between two famous parks
blocks.text: Down below, this highway corridor links Yellowstone directly with Grand Teton. For many visitors the two parks are effectively one vacation: geysers and bison one day, then the Teton skyline and Jackson Hole the next.

blocks.title: South Entrance
blocks.text: The south entrance area is just ahead. Crossing it means we are leaving Yellowstone National Park, but not the larger ecosystem; forests, wildlife and volcanic terrain continue without paying much attention to the park boundary.

blocks.title: The Tetons should start taking over the skyline
blocks.text: The Teton Range should begin asserting itself ahead-right now. This is the early acknowledgment: the mountains are too prominent to pretend they are not there, but we'll save most of the Teton story for the closer Jackson Lake pass.

blocks.title: Another heavily visited national park
blocks.text: Grand Teton National Park recorded about 3.8 million recreation visits in 2025, placing it among the ten most visited national parks. That means our short flight is connecting two parks that together drew more than eight and a half million visits in one year.

blocks.title: Jackson Lake ahead
blocks.text: Jackson Lake is becoming the major foreground feature, with the Tetons rising beyond it to the right. The combination of water, broad valley and abrupt mountain wall is one of the classic views associated with the park.

blocks.title: Why Jackson Hole is called a hole
blocks.text: The name Jackson Hole comes from the fur-trade era. Mountain men used the word hole for a broad valley surrounded by mountains, and this one became associated with trapper David Jackson. The beaver trade faded, but the name stuck.

blocks.title: Jackson Lake and the Tetons
blocks.text: This is the main Jackson Lake viewing window. Keep the Teton Range off the right side. The peaks should be well established in view now, not something first introduced as they slip behind. Let the lake provide the foreground and the mountain wall provide the scale.

blocks.title: South along the Teton front
blocks.text: We are continuing south with the Tetons off the right side. The central peaks should remain visually dominant for much of this leg, gradually shifting from abeam toward right-rear as we approach the airport.

blocks.title: A valley built around scenery
blocks.text: Tourism now shapes nearly everything about Jackson Hole's public image: skiing, wildlife watching, national parks, dude-ranch history and a downtown designed to feel unmistakably western. The landscape is the attraction, but the surrounding economy grew around helping visitors experience it.

blocks.title: An airport inside a national park
blocks.text: Jackson Hole Airport has an unusual distinction: it is the only commercial airport in the United States located entirely inside a national park. Commercial service began here before the park reached its modern boundaries, so the airport effectively found itself inside Grand Teton as the protected area expanded.

blocks.title: Wyoming's busiest airport
blocks.text: Despite the mountain setting and one runway, Jackson Hole is the busiest airport in Wyoming. For airline passengers, landing here can be a sightseeing experience of its own because the Tetons are visible almost immediately from the terminal and ramp.

blocks.title: The Tetons moving toward the rear quarter
blocks.text: The main Teton wall should now be shifting toward the right-rear as we continue south. If you want one last long look, this is the time; the arrival is starting to take over the flight.

blocks.title: Jackson Hole Airport
blocks.text: Jackson Hole Airport is coming up ahead at about 6,450 feet elevation. I'll leave you to the landing from here. When you're down and finished with the flight, say Trip destination. That will also stop the microphone and freeze the diagnostic log so you can review it afterward.
